summary:
Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or trans identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, added by social Christian legislators to a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape and signed by President Violeta Chamorro in July 1992, punished anyone who would "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner" with up to three years' imprisonment; the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality appeal in March 1994. The provision was dropped when the new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008. Its vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work.

Formal legality does not translate into protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Nicaragua documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived opponents of the government that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among the year's significant human rights violations. The official US assessment places anti-LGBTI abuse inside a broader climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International's May 2019 reporting situates that climate in the crackdown on protests that began in April 2018, which the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights credited with at least 325 deaths and more than 2,000 injuries. The journalist Miguel Mora described being beaten by a pro-government mob and said he was targeted partly for being gay, an account that ties political repression to homophobia. Media in Nicaragua has been restricted since the 2018 protests, which limits coverage of LGBT issues.

Violence against LGBT people is generally culturally accepted and legally unenforced, and attacks go largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes. A 2012 survey by the Center for Justice and International Law counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, among them 15 murders covering 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with the true figure expected to be higher. The feminist organisation Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime or murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person in the first two quarters of 2024. Trans women are the most targeted group, and state police are among the aggressors, tied with family members in 2022.

Discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is barred in several settings, though enforcement is not documented. Article 315 of the Penal Code, covering offences against labour rights, punishes employment discrimination based on "sexual option" by up to one year in prison; Article 3(l) of Law N° 820 prohibits discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds in the HIV and AIDS context; Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 bars it in access to health services on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression; and Article 36(5) of the Penal Code makes sexual-orientation discrimination an aggravating circumstance when any criminal offence is committed.

Relationship recognition is closed to same-sex couples. In June 2014 the Nicaraguan Congress approved a revised Family Code limiting marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples, which took effect on 8 April 2015, and several organisations filed an action of unconstitutionality against it. Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration measures including marriage; no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is largely opposed to legal equality. A Pew survey conducted from 9 November to 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed to same-sex marriage, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support.

Visibility is uneven along gender lines. Gay men are generally more visible in public than lesbians, who often socialise privately. An annual Gay Pride celebration has been held in Managua around 28 June since the country's first public pride festival in 1991, in a context where political gatherings have been heavily restricted since 2018.

Suppression of independent media since the 2018 protests constrains reporting on LGBT issues generally, which bears on how much violence or discrimination becomes publicly documented.

The Francis and Morgan Global Barometers entry for Nicaragua records no documented finding for this jurisdiction, so it neither corroborates nor contradicts the evidence drawn from government and human-rights sources.
localsOnly:
Residents face a gap between written protections and their use. The penal code's employment discrimination offence, the HIV-context prohibition in Law N° 820 and Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 on health services exist on the statute books, but the sources record no prosecutions or enforcement outcomes under them.

Same-sex households receive none of the legal benefits and protections attached to opposite-sex marriage under the Family Code in force since 8 April 2015, and the constitutional definition in Article 72 leaves no domestic route to recognition. The action of unconstitutionality filed by several organisations against the Family Code has no recorded outcome in the sources.

Reporting of attacks is suppressed by fear. NGOs record that victims seldom come forward because of possible retaliation and poor legal outcomes, so monitoring counts by the Center for Justice and International Law and by Programa Feminista La Corriente are understood to understate the real number of aggressions, and the same undercount applies to police involvement.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state whether legal gender recognition is available, what markers Nicaraguan passports or identity documents carry for trans travellers, or how arrival screening treats gender presentation. Nothing in the inventory addresses these.

Unresolved: the outcome of the unconstitutionality challenge to the Family Code is not recorded, and no source confirms whether Nicaragua has taken any step to implement the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018; the inventory states only that no implementation is recorded.

Unresolved: no youth-specific or visitor-specific health-care access findings are recorded, and no source documents enforcement convictions under the discrimination provisions cited.

The casualty and injury totals for the post-April-2018 crackdown are attributed to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights as reported by Amnesty International; the inventory does not carry a later update to those figures.
